extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (examiner drafting/reply guidance on 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness rejections)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting legally sufficient obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103: how to cite references, map claimed elements to prior art, and supply the factual/legal rationale (from references, common knowledge, business practice, official notice, or precedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good statement of the rejection (structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim X is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Reference A in view of Reference B. Identify which reference teaches each claimed element, state what elements are not taught, and explain why it would have been obvious to combine or modify the references to obtain the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an explicit mapping of claimed elements to teachings of the applied reference(s). State the missing element(s) and supply a reasoned rationale why a person of ordinary skill would have made the modification or combination (e.g., to obtain an expected advantage, to prevent error, to streamline a business process). Use concrete citations to the references when possible and show the logical link; avoid mere conclusory statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale implicitly contained in a reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a reference implicitly suggests the claimed modification, the examiner may rely on that implicit teaching as the rationale supporting an obviousness rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how the reference's disclosure implies the added steps or modification (e.g., security/authorization is implied when matching account holder ID/password). Show why the implicit teaching would lead the ordinary artisan to the claimed feature rather than merely asserting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale reasoned from common knowledge in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Rationales based on what is 'old and well established' in the relevant business/technical community may support an obviousness rejection when properly explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on bare conclusions. Provide a factual explanation or example demonstrating the common practice (e.g., use of credit card payment on the Internet, customer surveys for service feedback). Make clear why the ordinary artisan would have applied that common practice to the reference's system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale reasoned from established business principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Established business practices and principles (e.g., customer service surveys, price-matching promotions) can supply the motivation to modify prior art to include claimed steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the business principle and why it would be applicable to the reference system; explain that the practice is well known in commerce and would have been an obvious adaptation to the prior-art teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale reasoned from official notice
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may take Official Notice of facts that are well known and not subject to reasonable dispute to support an obviousness rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When taking Official Notice, provide illustrative examples or commonplace analogies (the manual pizza-order verification example) to show the fact is well known and explain why it makes the claimed modification obvious. Do not merely state Official Notice without supplying supporting factual context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design choice / lacks advantage is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple statement that a claimed difference is a 'design choice' or 'lacks an advantage or unexpected result' is not an adequate factual rationale for an obviousness rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conclusory language. Instead, supply objective reasoning or evidence showing why the modification would have been made by one of ordinary skill (e.g., expected advantages, industry routine, technical motivation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automation of a known manual process (legal precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely automating manual steps known in the prior art (providing a computer to perform the same function) is generally insufficient to establish patentability; automation alone often yields no enhancement beyond speed or convenience (In re Venner guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that automating a manual process gives the expected results and therefore may be obvious. To support patentability, show that the automation provides a non-obvious improvement (e.g., new technical effect or unexpected result) beyond mere speed/automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automation on the Internet (legal precedent applied to networked implementations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing a known manual process on the Internet (or adding Internet-based retrieval/communication) will often be obvious where the only change is networked automation and the advantages (global reach, convenience) are the expected result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show why incorporating Internet-based features would have been an obvious application of existing practices (cite references showing Internet surveying, remote retrieval, etc.) unless there is a demonstrated inventive improvement beyond expected network advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-functional data differences on an article of manufacture do not patentably distinguish
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences that reside solely in the non-functional data stored on a medium (labels, content fields that do not change the substrate's function) do not make an article of manufacture patentably distinct from prior art (In re Gulack, In re Lowry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that merely storing different descriptive data in the same data-field structure is an obvious labeling/design choice and does not impart patentability; show why the data is not functionally related to the substrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content/subjective meaning of stored queries or data does not patentably distinguish a known system
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific meaning or subjective interpretation of queries/data loaded onto a known networked system generally will not patentably distinguish that system from prior art; the network/system remains the same even if the content changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on structural/functional differences in the machine or network rather than on the semantic content of stored queries. Explain why changing the content does not alter the system's patentable characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known system/machine with computer program — mere implementation without functional improvement is not inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting a known system on a programmed computer (or adding software that merely performs the same manual steps) is often unpatentable absent an inventive improvement in functionality, performance, or technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate whether the claimed program provides more than expected automation (e.g., a new algorithmic technique producing an unexpected technical result). If it does not, explain why a skilled artisan would simply have automated the manual process and thus it is obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete examples/evidence when asserting 'well known' practices
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on common practices, business routines, or Official Notice, support assertions with concrete examples (textbooks, training manuals, commonly known practices) to show the fact is widely recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite specific prior art, manuals, textbooks, or give real-world examples (e.g., customer-survey emails, price-matching with proof via URLs) to substantiate the assertion that the practice was known and would have been applied to the reference.
